content:
Now that we're in the era of "abundant AI development power", I think a very cool project would be a complete implementation of the Risch algorithm. It's (in a meaningful sense) the most complete symbolic integration possible, and it's sufficiently complicated with enough edge cases that it's never been fully completed. Programs like Mathematica, Macsyma, Axiom, etc. all have partial implementations. I think a fantastic project would be:

-Set up enough of a CAS basis in Lean to express the task
-Implement the Risch algorithm
-Step 1 of verification: Verify its correctness (any expression it returns is a true antiderivative of the input)
-Step 2: Verify its completeness (if an elementary integrand exists, it will find it).

I think that would be an impressive tour de force of how Lean enables verified AI-assisted software development.

(Small note, the completeness is only provable assuming Schaunel's conjecture. Which I think is an acceptable hypothesis to take. :slight_smile: )

Note that Risch is well-known to produce incorrect anti-derivatives. More precisely, Risch solves the algebraic problem as defined, but produces analytically incorrect answers.

Motto: analysis is not algebra.

Sure, but honestly that point makes it even more attractive for formalization I think! Getting antiderivatives that are numerically misleading is a classic footgun.

And, there is a rich body of work trying to make outputs match up in both senses, like Rioboo's which fixes the case of arctan of a rational function to avoid any unnecessary discontinuities.

With formalization we can, first, validate the choices of branch cuts etc which are often a first source of error. So that locally derivatives are correct. Then the main issue is when the antiderivative has jump discontinuities at a point where the integrand was integrable (or at least, continuous).

So, we could return an additional (provably correct) Bool, with the antiderivative, indicating "Can we prove that this is only discontinuous at points where the input is too?". And ideally, with research, we could make this always return true and dispense with it so that is a valid algebraic and analytic integral.

Absolutely: doing Risch 'right', returning more information that could be used to do the analysis correctly would be amazing. Renaud (Rioboo) would be pleased to see his work furthered. Certainly trying to 'fix up' the answers from Risch post-facto using limits turned out to be way harder than the original integration problem (said as one of the people who had to work hard in Maple to fix various bugs due to just that.)

Rubi (Rule-based Integrator) could be used as a rich source of test cases, to at least discover such discrepencies (and probably correct candidates) for further triage and examinination.

Also I wonder if there is some verification asymmetry here, so a algebraically produced integral result is easy to verify its analytical correctness (prove or disprove by an automated tactic), and a disproof or a prove failure produce useful signals for the fix.
My hunch would be that arxiv#1109.2809 contains useful ideas in pursuit of this goal. Because the problem is always due to branch cuts.
